figures.alt: Five spike marks share a time axis with an activation trace. Each mark aligns with a vertical rise of one activation unit. The activation decays smoothly between spikes, and nearby spikes build on the remaining activation.
figures.caption: Figure 2.1: Each spike adds one activation unit, which then decays with a 50 ms time constant. Closely spaced spikes add to the activation left by earlier spikes. The five spike times are an illustrative input, and the activation is calculated exactly from the chapter equation.

figures.alt: As theta increases through the interior from minus 20 to 20 activation units, r1 increases toward 200 spikes per second and r2 decreases toward zero. Their dashed sum stays at 200. A lower aligned plot shows D constant at 100 coordinate units squared per second. Open endpoint circles exclude both boundaries.
figures.caption: Figure 2.3: For the chapter’s two mutually inhibiting cells, b = 20 activation units and tau = 0.1 s give opposite changes in the two rates. Their sum remains 200 spikes/s, so local D remains 100 coordinate units squared/s. Open endpoints mark the excluded boundaries; the linear interior model does not determine boundary behavior. These curves are calculated examples, not simulation data.

figures.alt: Wrapped Gaussian densities at 0.2, 1 and 5 seconds broaden toward a dashed uniform density over angular errors from minus pi to pi. Below, line mean squared error rises linearly while wrapped angular mean squared error approaches a horizontal pi squared over three reference, with the same constant diffusion coefficient.
figures.caption: Figure 2.4: With the same constant D = 0.5 rad²/s, wrapped Gaussian error densities widen toward 1/(2π). The unbounded line has mean squared error 2Dt; reporting angular error in [−𝜋,𝜋) instead gives a mean squared error that approaches π²/3. The flattening comes from the bounded error convention while local diffusion stays constant. All curves are analytic teaching calculations, not paper simulation data.
